title: The Stuffy-Nose Taster
briefing: Keisha, 14, has a cold and a completely blocked nose. Her favourite strawberry yogurt tastes like “sweet nothing”, and with her eyes closed she can't tell a slice of apple from a slice of potato. She can still tell that lemon is sour and chips are salty.
question: Where did the flavour of Keisha's food go?

clues.title: Blocked nose
clues.text: Keisha can't breathe through her nose at all. She doesn't notice the toast burning in the kitchen until she sees the smoke.

clues.title: Sweet nothing
clues.text: Her strawberry yogurt tastes sweet, but not like strawberry. Lemon still tastes sour and chips still taste salty.
clues.shows: the tongue's basic tastes still working while the rest of the flavour is missing

clues.title: Apple or potato?
clues.text: With her eyes closed she can't tell a slice of apple from a slice of raw potato. Both are just “crunchy and a bit sweet”.
clues.shows: two different foods becoming impossible to tell apart once smell is gone

clues.title: Back to normal
clues.text: Three days later her nose clears. The first spoonful of the same yogurt tastes of strawberries again.
clues.shows: flavour coming back the moment smell does

hypotheses.text: Being ill has damaged her tongue.
hypotheses.flaw: Her tongue still tastes sweet, salty and sour perfectly well — only the strawberry part is missing, and it came back the moment her nose cleared.
Every food lost its flavour at once, not just the yogurt — and the same yogurt tasted normal three days later.

hypotheses.text: She's too tired to notice what she's eating.
hypotheses.flaw: She noticed sweet, sour and salty without any trouble; only the flavours that come from smell disappeared.

hypotheses.text: Most of what we call flavour is actually smell: smells from food drift up the back of the throat to the nose. With her nose blocked, only the tongue's basic tastes — like sweet, salty and sour — get through.

prediction.prompt: As Keisha's nose gets more and more blocked — from clear to completely stuffed — what happens to how much flavour she notices?

second.question: And the basic sweet and sour tastes from her tongue?

transfer.context: Leo holds his nose and eats a jellybean. It just tastes sweet. When he lets go of his nose, it suddenly tastes of cherry.
options: Letting go let cherry smells from his mouth reach his nose, adding flavour to the sweet taste his tongue already had.
Holding his nose stopped his tongue working.
The jellybean changed flavour as it melted.
He swallowed too fast to taste it.
transfer.retryHint: Sweet but no flavour, then flavour back the moment the nose opens — which of Keisha's clues matches that?
transfer.explanation: Leo's tongue tasted 'sweet' the whole time. The cherry part is a smell: once he let go, smell molecules from the jellybean drifted up the back of his throat to his nose and the flavour appeared — exactly what happened when Keisha's nose cleared.

takeaway: Flavour is a team effort. Your tongue senses only a few basic tastes; the rest comes from smells that drift up the back of your throat to your nose. Block the nose and food tastes flat.
